levels.headline: Burnham signs EU deals worth up to £17bn a year and plans a national conversation on Brexit
levels.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham signed a package of deals with the European Union at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. They cover food and drink, a link between carbon markets and a youth experience scheme. The government says the deals are worth up to £17 billion a year and could add up to 0.5% to UK economic output (GDP) by 2040.
Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, accused Burnham of betraying Brexit voters by bringing Britain back into parts of the EU single market. Before the summit Burnham said Brexit has not worked.
Burnham has said a referendum on rejoining the EU is possible in a future election manifesto, but that it would not be the right thing to do now. Soon after the summit he will open a national conversation on Britain's long-term relationship with the EU. He became prime minister after Keir Starmer resigned.
levels.why: It could change how easily Britain trades with Europe, and it reopens the biggest argument in British politics of the last ten years.

It was the best day for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025. Tuesday's session had not finished at the time of writing.

levels.headline: UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, ONS says, with services leading the way
levels.body:
The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the third quarter of 2026, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said in its first estimate, published on 12 November. That is up from growth of 0.5% in the previous quarter. The figure matched forecasts, and the ONS said services were the main driver, growing 0.9%. As a first estimate it can still be revised, and the next release is due on 22 December.
Chancellor John Healey called it the fastest growth in almost ten years outside the pandemic. CNBC reported that artificial intelligence was providing an extra engine of growth.
Some economists are more cautious. JP Morgan's Scott Gardner expects the economy's strength to be tested in the coming months. The Bank of England has raised interest rates to 4% and has warned inflation could approach 5%.
levels.why: Growth helps pay for jobs, wages and public services, but the Bank of England is also worried about prices.

levels.headline: Brent oil dips to about $89 as Iran claims three more tankers hit mines in Hormuz
levels.body:
Brent crude futures dipped to about $89.2 a barrel on Tuesday 24 November, while US West Texas Intermediate fell to about $80.1. That is well below an October high of nearly $105 for Brent. A Eurasia Group analyst expects Brent to stay in the lower half of an $80 to $100 range, but warns that escalating Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz could reverse that.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said three tankers hit mines in the strait, despite US air cover and escorts. The claim has not been independently confirmed, and the US military disputed similar claims earlier.
On Monday the US Treasury widened sanctions on more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and key people, in what it called an effort to disrupt Iran's shadow banking networks.
levels.why: Oil prices feed straight into petrol, diesel and heating costs, and into the inflation that the Bank of England is trying to control.

levels.headline: Home Secretary sets out tougher rules for migrants who want to settle in the UK
levels.body:
The government has set out new rules for migrants who want to settle permanently in the UK, replacing near-automatic settlement after long residence with an earned model. The default qualifying period becomes 10 years. The highest earners can settle after 3 years, while people earning above £50,271 and some public servants, such as doctors, nurses and teachers, can do so after 5. People who have broken immigration rules face at least 20 years.
Care workers who met their visa conditions and earned at least £25,000 can settle after 5 years. Applicants need a clean criminal record, English at a set standard, no debts owed to the taxpayer and sustained National Insurance contributions.
Settled status will not be taken from anyone who already has it. The government estimates that over 500,000 people will wait longer than 5 years. Reform has pledged to scrap indefinite leave to remain.

headline: Belgian national strike grounds flights as 50,000 march against austerity

terms.meaning: Government policies that cut spending or raise taxes to reduce debt.

levels.headline: Belgian national strike grounds flights as 50,000 march against austerity
levels.body:
A national strike in Belgium on Monday 23 November grounded all flights and disrupted public transport, schools and other public services, Euronews reported. Police said 50,000 people marched through the capital, Brussels, to protest against government austerity measures.
The government wants to save €10 billion over the next few years to reduce Belgium's high budget deficit. Unions want higher taxes on high earners instead. Divisions remain within the coalition. Prime Minister Bart De Wever offered his resignation to the king on 2 November over the budget impasse, but the king refused to accept it and gave him more time to find a solution.
Euronews described the government's future as hanging in the balance. Earlier rounds of the protest movement include a national strike in October that police said drew some 30,000 people.
levels.why: It shows how hard it is for governments in Europe to cut deficits without losing public support, and Belgium hosts the EU's main institutions.
